summary.text: 起 is analyzed as a compound of 走, which contributes movement, and 巳, which supplies a sound cue. Its transmitted gloss is “able to stand”; documented uses include standing, rising, setting out, mobilizing troops and beginning.

formation.text: The transmitted analysis is phonosemantic: 走 contributes movement and 巳 supplies the sound. The account glosses 起 as “able to stand.” A later philological interpretation proposes that the graph originally referred to setting out a step, but this is not confirmed by a secure early form.

components.text: 走 contributes movement in the transmitted analysis. Reported Chu manuscript forms use 辵 with 己; their relation to the transmitted graphic form is not established.
巳 is the sound element in the transmitted analysis. Reported Chu forms instead use 己 as the sound element; the available Old Chinese reconstructions for 巳 differ.

sound_limitation.text: The cited reconstructions offer comparisons but do not give a complete sound derivation or establish how close the pronunciations were when the graph was formed.

sound.text: The supplied current-reading rows give 巳 sì and 起 qǐ in Modern Mandarin. This pair does not establish their historical sound relationship.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart table gives 巳 MC ziX and 起 MC khiX; this comparison does not by itself prove the phonetic analysis.
The supplied Baxter–Sagart table gives 巳 OC *s-[ɢ]əʔ and 起 OC *C.qʰ(r)əʔ. Another source gives different Old Chinese forms for 巳; the discrepancy is unresolved.

history.text: The transmitted seal-script analysis presents 起 as 走 plus 巳. Reported Chu manuscript forms use 辵 plus 己, with both 己 and 巳 described as possible sound elements. The selected seal-style image is a modern redraw, not an ancient inscription.

A proposed Warring States bronze graph has been read as 走 plus ◎, but its identification as 起 is questioned because the second element resembles 卩 rather than 巳. It is not a secure stage in the written history.

Traditional explanations picture a snake raising its head or propose that 起 originally referred to setting out a step. Neither account is confirmed by a secure early form; the supposed snake’s name and sound are not established.

uncertainties.text: No secure oracle-bone form or precisely dated earliest use is identified. The Chu manuscript phrase is useful early evidence, but its date and status as the earliest attested use remain unresolved.

senses.text: The transmitted gloss is “able to stand,” and classical citations document standing up. They do not establish this as the earliest use or original meaning.
Classical citations and dictionary definitions document rising or getting up, including rising from sitting or lying. They do not date this use relative to other meanings.
Classical citations attest 起 used for beginning. A later philological interpretation treats this as an extension, but its timing and path through intermediate meanings are unresolved.
A classical citation documents a use for departure. Its chronology relative to standing, rising or beginning is unresolved.
In the Chu manuscript phrase 天下之兵大起, 起 is interpreted as troops being raised or mobilized. The cited account gives no precise date and does not identify this as the earliest sense.

senses.gloss: rise; stand up; go up; begin
senses.text: These are recorded current meanings; their relative chronology is not established.

developments.text: A later philological interpretation proposes that “begin” developed from “stand.” The citations do not establish a dated path between these uses.

limitations.text: No use in the earliest documented corpus or period is securely identified. The Chu manuscript citation has no precise date in the cited account. The proposed step-setting original meaning is an interpretation, not an established earliest attestation.
Classical citations attest standing, rising, beginning, departure, occurrence and mobilization, but do not establish their chronological sequence or a continuous path of semantic change.

overview.text: 起 combines a movement element with a sound element. Its transmitted gloss is “able to stand”; common meanings include rise, get up, go up and begin.

components.text: 走 contributes movement to the character.
巳 supplies the sound in the transmitted analysis; reported Chu forms use 己 in this role.

relationships.text: 走 contributes movement in the transmitted analysis of 起; it is identified as semantic, not phonetic.

The transmitted analysis identifies 巳 as phonetic. Baxter–Sagart gives same-period Middle and Old Chinese comparisons for 巳 and 起; another source gives a different Old Chinese transcription for 巳. These comparisons do not establish a complete sound derivation.
